# Actual depth maximization over the unequal-endpoint selector body

This is a necessary finite system for the three-fiber problem. It combines
the endpoint selector with actual minimum caps and their full section
centroids. It does not prove the missing cap-budget inequality or OC.

Let d>=1. Let A,B,C be convex bodies in R^d, placed respectively at
integer indices -1,0,1, with (A+C)/2 contained in B. Write

    a=|A|, b=|B|, c=|C|, M=a+b+c,
    0<a<c, c<a+b, b<a+c.

The mixed measure mu is unnormalized fiber volume. For y in B, let

    f(y)=inf{mu(H): H is a closed ambient halfspace containing (0,y)}.

Define the compact convex selector body

    Y={ [b g_B+a g_A+integral x d sigma]/(b+2a):
                      0<=sigma<=1_C dx, sigma(C)=a }.             (1)

The results about this body and lower-cap selection are proved in
`candidate 0acdf1c3867a889d`, section 1. In
particular Y is nonempty and compact, and every point of Y has depth at
least gamma_d(b+2a)/2. Also Y is uniformly inside B: every such point is
(b g_B+2a g_eta)/(b+2a), with g_eta in B, so an interior ball of radius
(b/(b+2a)) dist(g_B, boundary B) is available at every point of Y.

## 1. The finite section-selector theorem

Let y_* maximize f on Y, and put D=f(y_*). Suppose D<M/2. There exist
k<=d+1 actual minimum caps

    H_j={ (z,x): u_j.(x-y_*)+v_j z>=0 },   |u_j|=1,
    mu(H_j)=D,                                                   (2)

positive weights omega_j summing to one, and effective section measures
tau_jz on K_z intersect boundary H_j (K_-1=A,K_0=B,K_1=C), with the
following properties. Put

    S_jz=tau_jz(R^d), X_jz=integral x d tau_jz,
    S_j=sum_z S_jz, X_j=sum_z X_jz.

Each tau_jz equals ordinary (d-1)-dimensional section measure when the
hyperplane properly cuts the interior of K_z, is zero when disjoint from
K_z, and on a supporting face is theta_jz times its (d-1)-dimensional
measure for a measurable 0<=theta_jz<=1. A supporting face of dimension
less than d-1 contributes zero. THE SAME theta_jz is used in both mass
and all first moments. Then

    S_j>0,
    S_j,-1=S_j,1,
    X_j=S_j y_*,                                               (3)

and the vector

    u_bar=sum_j omega_j S_j u_j                                (4)

satisfies

    u_bar.(y-y_*)>=0 for all y in Y.                            (5)

Thus every effective full ambient section has centroid (0,y_*).
If u_bar!=0, the selector producing y_* in (1) is uniquely the actual
uniform lower a-volume cap

    sigma_*=1_(C intersect {u_bar.x<=t}) dx,
    |C intersect {u_bar.x<=t}|=a.                              (6)

If u_bar=0, (4) gives a positive section-weighted normal balance; in
that case no assertion that the selector is an indicator is made.

All the caps in (2) minimize the original ambient cap mass at the SAME
point. They are not shifted low-mass cover caps. Boundary coincidences
are retained in (3) through the effective section traces.

## 2. Compact cap parameters and local Lipschitz continuity

Work on a bounded open neighborhood U of Y whose closure is inside B.
Every nonvertical cap containing (0,y) can be shrunk to one through it,
so its mass is no smaller than that of some

    H(y,u,v)={ (z,x): u.(x-y)+vz>=0 }, |u|=1.

Choose L exceeding sup{|x-y|:x in A union B union C, y in closure U}
by two. If v>=L-1, the C cap is full and the A cap empty. If v<=-L+1,
the reverse holds. Thus clipping v to [-L+1,L-1] does not change its
mass outside that interval. We may optimize over the compact parameter
space sphere^(d-1) times [-L,L], and choose each active representative
in its interior with respect to the v coordinate.

A vertical cap containing the middle fiber has mass at least
min(a+b,b+c)>M/2. The two opposite nonvertical caps through any y have
masses summing to M, because their boundaries have zero d-volume in
all fibers. Hence a nonvertical cap of mass <=M/2 always exists, and

    f(y)=min_(|u|=1, |v|<=L) F(y,u,v),
    F(y,u,v)=sum_z |K_z intersect H(y,u,v)|.                    (7)

This equality holds throughout U. The minimum is attained.

The function F is jointly locally Lipschitz, uniformly on the compact
parameter set. Indeed changing its parameters by epsilon changes the
membership of a bounded fiber only in an O(epsilon)-thick slab about
its original cutting plane. Projection of every fiber onto that plane
has uniformly bounded (d-1)-volume; Cavalieri therefore bounds the
changed volume by O(epsilon). A finite collection of sphere charts
gives uniform constants. The minimum in (7) is consequently locally
Lipschitz in y. It is continuous, so f has the claimed maximizer on Y.

## 3. A marginal-function generalized-gradient lemma

For a locally Lipschitz function h on Euclidean space, write partial_C h
for its Clarke generalized gradient: the closed convex hull of limits
of ordinary gradients at differentiability points tending to the point
in question. Rademacher's theorem supplies these differentiability
points. This is a nonempty compact convex set. The same definition in
smooth local coordinates applies to the sphere parameter.

We use the following elementary marginal lemma. Suppose

    h(y)=min_(p in P) G(y,p),

with compact P, locally Lipschitz G uniformly in p, and all active
parameters representable in the interior of smooth local charts. Then
every gradient limit g used in defining partial_C h(y_*) has an active
p_* such that

    (g,0) belongs to partial_C G(y_*,p_*).                     (8)

Proof. Choose differentiability points y_l tending to y_* with
grad h(y_l) tending to g, and active p_l. Pass to p_l tending to p_*
and use a single local chart. Activity passes to the limit by continuity.
For all nearby y,p,

 G(y,p)-G(y_l,p_l)>=h(y)-h(y_l)
                 =grad h(y_l).(y-y_l)+o(|y-y_l|).

Thus (grad h(y_l),0) is a Frechet subgradient of G at (y_l,p_l), and
therefore is in its Clarke generalized gradient. For completeness, the
last implication follows by separation: if a Frechet subgradient lies
outside the closed convex hull of nearby gradient limits, some direction
separates it strictly from all nearby ordinary gradients. Integrating
those directional bounds on parallel lines, then using continuity to
reach the line through the point, contradicts the Frechet lower bound.
The Clarke generalized gradient has closed graph under bounded limits,
directly from its definition by convex hulls of gradients in shrinking
neighborhoods. Passing to the limit proves (8).

It follows that partial_C h(y_*) is contained in the convex hull of the
vectors g arising in (8). This lemma is stronger than selecting a
partial-y gradient arbitrarily: all p-components vanish simultaneously
in the SAME joint generalized gradient.

## 4. Consistent section traces for cap gradients

Apply the lemma to F in (7). Its ordinary coarea differential, at proper
cuts, has the following components in the coordinates (y,v,u):

    g_y=-S u,
    g_v=sum_z z S_z,
    g_u=proj_(u-perp)(sum_z X_z-S y).                         (9)

Here S_z and X_z are respectively section mass and first moment. This
follows by moving the affine margin
u.(x-y)+vz: its first displacement is
du.(x-y)-u.dy+z dv, and the coarea factor is 1/|u|=1.

At a supporting facet, the corresponding joint generalized-gradient
contribution still has (9), using a single measurable trace density
0<=theta_z<=1 for its mass and every first moment. One direct
justification is to approach by ordinary differentiability parameters.
Project the approaching section orthogonally to the limiting plane.
The projected section indicators are bounded by one, and the surface
pushforward density differs from that indicator by a Jacobian factor
tending to one. All weak limits are supported on the limiting face.
They therefore have densities between zero and one there. A proper cut
has full density one, since its relative boundary has (d-1)-measure zero
and interior section points persist. Convex combinations and weak limits
retain the same representation for mass and all moments. A disjoint cut
contributes zero. The sum rule for generalized gradients may enlarge
the admissible choices across fibers, but still gives this representation;
only existence of one representation is used here. The sum rule itself
follows by the same local directional separation, or by integrating the
separate almost-everywhere derivative bounds.

This argument also covers d=1: sections have H_0 mass, supporting
endpoints have a coefficient in [0,1], and the sphere has no tangent
coordinate. There is no untracked surface Jacobian in (9).

For a joint generalized gradient (g,0) supplied by (8), the vanishing
v component gives S_-1=S_1. The vanishing tangent-u component says
X-Sy is parallel to u. Every effective section point satisfies the exact
identity u.(x-y)+vz=0. Integrating it with the SAME trace densities gives

    u.(X-Sy)+v sum_z zS_z=0.

The already established v balance now gives X=Sy. Since y is interior
to B, its middle section is proper with positive (d-1)-volume, so S>0.
Consequently every g furnished by the marginal lemma has

    g=-Su

for an actual active cap equipped with the full centroid identities (3).

## 5. Constrained center maximization and finite selection

Let N_Y(y_*)={g:g.(y-y_*)<=0 for every y in Y}. At a local maximum
of a locally Lipschitz function h over a convex set Y,

    partial_C h(y_*) intersect N_Y(y_*) is nonempty.           (10)

Here is a direct version of the constrained necessary condition. If
the compact convex generalized-gradient set and the closed convex cone
N_Y were disjoint, strict separation would give a vector w in the
tangent cone of Y and a number epsilon>0 such that g.w>=epsilon for
every generalized gradient g. Approximate w by a positive multiple of
a feasible secant of Y, retaining a positive lower bound. All ordinary
gradients sufficiently near y_* then have a positive derivative in
this direction, by the definition of the generalized gradient. Integrate
along nearby parallel line segments and pass to the desired segment by
continuity. This makes h strictly increase on a feasible segment, a
contradiction. This proves (10), including boundary points of Y.

By sections 3 and 4, partial_C f(y_*) is contained in the convex hull
of vectors -S u from actual active caps satisfying (3). This latter
collection is compact: active cap parameters form a compact set, section
trace measures are weakly compact, and the linear zero-component
constraints are closed. Thus (10) and Caratheodory in R^d give at most
d+1 such caps and weights omega_j, with

    -sum_j omega_j S_j u_j in N_Y(y_*).

Discard zero weights. This is precisely (4)-(5). When u_bar is nonzero,
the support-minimizer formula for the moment body in (1) gives the
unique lower-cap selector (6). This completes the theorem.

## 6. The exact new constraint and its present limit

The earlier finite selector certificate only had the support relation
for an averaged normal; its caps could be shifted and need not be
minimum caps. Here the same selected point has equal-mass active caps,
each with equal endpoint effective sections and full section centroid
(0,y_*), together with lower-cap ordering in the section-weighted
averaged normal u_bar. These conditions hold at every actual maximizer
over Y below M/2, without a smoothness assumption on the bodies or their
cap-volume functions.

The identities do not by themselves estimate the unused endpoint mass
in every cap. In particular no replacement of individual cap indicators
by their averaged affine margin, no log-concavity assertion for a
transported target, and no unproved per-circuit gamma_d budget is used.

## 7. A proved lower-dimensional consequence for every effective section

Fix one cap and its consistent effective section measures from the
theorem. The affine cap plane has the parametrization

    (z,t) -> (z, y_*+t-vz u),        t in u-perp.

This map preserves (d-1)-volume within every integer fiber. Under these
coordinates the central section is a (d-1)-dimensional convex body L,
with uniform volume measure. The endpoint effective sections are
measures alpha and chi with densities at most one on their respective
convex sections, and they have equal mass s by (3). The midpoint of
their supports is contained in L by convexity of the original family.
Their combined first moment with uniform L is zero, again by (3).

For d>=2 and s>0, the Gaussian triangular-map proof in
`candidate 71bcdfc8eb8340c6` applies to any
two compactly supported densities bounded by one with equal mass s.
Uniformity of the densities was not used: after normalization and
Gaussian smoothing both densities are bounded by 1/s, and the midpoint
Jacobian inequality gives a midpoint measure eta of mass s with density
at most one. Its support lies in L, and its centroid is the mean of the
two endpoint centroids. Thus zero is the centroid of

    1_L dt+2 eta.

The density-sandwich theorem in dimension d-1 now gives, for every closed
halfspace J of the full affine cap plane containing (0,0),

  alpha(J_-1)+|L intersect J_0|+chi(J_1)
       >= |L intersect J_0|+eta(J_0)
       >= (gamma_(d-1)/2)(|L|+2s).                            (11)

The first inequality is the exact midpoint indicator inequality and
therefore also includes mass on boundary halfspaces. Vertical J may
instead be checked directly: a containing vertical halfspace has mass
at least |L|+s, which is at least half the total. If s=0, (3) says zero
is the ordinary centroid of L, and ordinary Grunbaum gives the stronger
factor gamma_(d-1).

For d=1 the effective section consists of at most three atoms with
weights (s,1,s), at the three integer indices. The depth of its middle
point is (1+s)/(1+2s)>=1/2=gamma_0/2, also covering s=0.

Consequently EVERY effective section furnished by the theorem has
mixed halfspace depth at least gamma_(d-1)/2 at its actual anchor,
including facet coincidences. This is not an assertion about arbitrary
mixed measures whose centroids happen to be mixed-integer points: the
equal endpoint masses and the uniform central section are essential to
the argument. No integration of (11) into the missing ambient cap-mass
bound is asserted here.

## 8. The full active-section intersection matrix

For any two active caps define

    P_jk=tau_j(H_k)/S_j,
    b_jk=tau_j(boundary H_k)/S_j,
    kappa=gamma_(d-1)/2,

where tau_j is the full effective section measure, with its integer
coordinate retained. Both H_k and its opposite closed halfspace contain
the section anchor. Applying (11) to both, and observing that their
section masses sum to S_j plus their common boundary mass, gives

    kappa<=P_jk<=min(1,1-kappa+b_jk).                   (12)

In particular P_jj=b_jj=1. When d>=2 and the continuous normals u_j,u_k
are not parallel, every integer-fiber boundary intersection has codimension
one inside that fiber's (d-1)-dimensional section. All effective measures
are absolutely continuous relative to those sections, so b_jk=0 and

    kappa<=P_jk<=1-kappa.                              (13)

The parallel-normal case has an exact formula, not merely an error term.
Write u_k=epsilon u_j, epsilon in {1,-1}. On the j-section its k-margin
is (v_k-epsilon v_j)z. If this coefficient is zero, P_jk=1. Otherwise
the k-cap includes the entire central section and exactly one of the
two equally weighted endpoint sections. Writing s=S_j,-1=S_j,1 gives

    P_jk=(S_j,0+s)/(S_j,0+2s),
    b_jk=S_j,0/(S_j,0+2s).                            (14)

The dominated midpoint law from section 7 proves s<=S_j,0. Hence the
nontrivial value in (14) lies in [2/3,1]. This also describes all pairs
when d=1. It includes s=0 without discarding the central-only sections.

Finally, for any nonnegative weights lambda_k summing to one, (12) and
P_jj=1 imply the exact cap-mixture bound

    (1/S_j) integral sum_k lambda_k 1_(H_k) d tau_j
          >=kappa+(1-kappa)lambda_j.                  (15)

These are constraints on the entire matrix of actual active caps, with
closed-boundary mass retained. They do not assert that a shape deformation
realizes this mixture as an objective derivative, and no ambient cap-volume
budget follows without such an additional proved mechanism.
